lessons.title: Population dynamics and policies

lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Define and calculate birth rate, death rate and natural increase
Explain population pyramids and population policies
reviewNotes: Statements on which stage sub-Saharan Africa occupies are general; check current syllabus phrasing.
Dependency-ratio age bands (under 15, 15–64, 65+) are the common convention; confirm which the examiner uses.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Key terms
blocks.md: **Birth rate** and **death rate** are births and deaths per 1000 people per year. **Natural increase** = birth rate − death rate (per 1000; divide by 10 for a percentage). **Fertility rate** is the average number of children per woman. **Life expectancy** is the average years a newborn is expected to live. **Dependency ratio** = (under 15 + 65 and over) ÷ (15 to 64) × 100.

blocks.title: Demographic transition
blocks.md: **Stage 1:** high birth and death rates, small growth. **Stage 2:** death rate falls (health, food), birth rate stays high: rapid growth, many countries in sub-Saharan Africa are in this stage or moving to stage 3. **Stage 3:** birth rate falls. **Stage 4:** both low, slow growth. Some add a stage 5 with declining population.

blocks.caption: Birth and death rates through the four stages.
blocks.alt: Two curves: the death rate falls first, the birth rate falls later, with four labelled stages.

blocks.title: Pyramids and policies
blocks.md: A pyramid with a **wide base** and sharply narrowing top shows high birth rates and a young population. A narrow base shows low birth rates and ageing. **Policies:** anti-natalist (family planning, girls’ education, later marriage), pro-natalist (child allowances) and policies on migration. Policies must respect rights and local cultures.

blocks.title: Frequent errors
blocks.md:
- Natural increase excludes migration.
- Growth of 26 per 1000 equals 2.6%, not 26%.
- Population density (people per km²) differs from total population.
- A young population creates a high dependency ratio because many dependants are children.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Natural increase
blocks.statement: A region has a birth rate of 38 per 1000 and a death rate of 12 per 1000. Find the natural increase as a percentage.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Dependency ratio
blocks.statement: In a country 44% of people are under 15, 53% aged 15 to 64 and 3% aged 65 or more (illustrative figures). Find the dependency ratio.

lessons.title: Migration and urbanisation

objectives: Define migration and classify its types
Explain push and pull factors and the effects of rural-urban migration
Describe urban problems in African cities and ways of managing them
reviewNotes: Urban growth statements for Cameroon are qualitative; add current statistics only from official sources.
Check whether the syllabus asks for named models of migration (for example Lee’s model).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Migration
blocks.md: **Migration** is a permanent or semi-permanent change of residence. It can be **internal** or **international**, **voluntary** or **forced** (refugees, internally displaced people). **Push factors** drive people away (poverty, land shortage, insecurity, disasters); **pull factors** attract them (jobs, schools, services). **Obstacles** include cost, distance and lack of information.

blocks.title: Urbanisation
blocks.md: **Urbanisation** is the increase in the share of people living in towns. **Urban growth** is the rise in the number of town dwellers. Africa is urbanising rapidly because of rural-urban migration and natural increase in towns such as Douala and Yaoundé. Rapid growth outpaces housing, water, sanitation, transport and jobs.

blocks.caption: Push factors in the village and pull factors in the town.
blocks.alt: Two boxes joined by an arrow; the village box lists push factors and the town box lists pull factors.

blocks.title: Urban problems and responses
blocks.md: Typical problems: informal settlements with poor sanitation, traffic congestion, unemployment and a large informal sector, waste, flooding on low or built-over land, pressure on schools and health care. Responses: slum upgrading, planned housing, public transport, drainage, waste collection, and developing small and medium towns to share growth.

blocks.title: Be precise
blocks.md:
- Do not call all migrants ‘refugees’: a refugee is forced across an international border.
- Rural-urban migration also affects villages (loss of young workers, remittances).
- Urban growth is not the same as urbanisation.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Classify
blocks.statement: A young man leaves a village near Bafoussam to look for work in Douala. Classify the move and give one push and one pull factor.
steps: He stays in the same country: internal migration.
Push: few jobs in the village. Pull: more jobs in the port city.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Effects on the village
blocks.statement: Give two effects of rural-urban migration on the village of origin.
steps: Fewer young adults means less farm labour and an older population.
Migrants may send money (remittances), which pays for school fees and housing.
Fewer people can reduce pressure on land.
blocks.answer: Labour loss and ageing, but also remittances.

reviewNotes: Regional crop distribution is simplified: verify with the syllabus case studies.

blocks.title: Types of farming
blocks.md: **Subsistence** farming feeds the family (cassava, plantain, maize, yams, groundnuts), often on small plots with shifting cultivation or bush fallow. **Commercial** farming sells the produce: plantations of banana, rubber, oil palm and tea; smallholder **cash crops** such as cocoa, coffee and cotton. **Pastoral** farming keeps cattle, mainly in the northern savanna and western highlands.

blocks.title: Factors
blocks.md: **Physical:** temperature, rainfall and its reliability, soil, relief and drainage. **Human:** markets and prices, transport, capital and credit, land tenure, technology, government policy, labour. Cocoa suits the humid south, coffee the cooler western highlands, cotton the drier north; volcanic soils help plantations near Mount Cameroon.

items.text: Availability: enough food is produced or imported
Access: people can afford or reach it
Utilisation: safe, nutritious food, clean water
Stability: supply is reliable through the year

blocks.caption: The four dimensions of food security.
blocks.alt: Four stacked boxes naming availability, access, utilisation and stability.

blocks.title: Food security
blocks.md: Food security means all people have enough safe, nutritious food at all times. It has four dimensions: **availability, access, utilisation, stability**. Threats: poor roads, post-harvest losses, climate variability, pests, conflict, low incomes. Responses: better seeds, storage, irrigation, farm roads, cooperatives, processing, and training.

blocks.title: Mistakes to avoid
blocks.md:
- Subsistence farming can include selling a small surplus: it is defined by the main purpose.
- Yield = production ÷ area, not total production.
- Food security is not only about producing more: access and storage matter.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Yield
blocks.statement: A farmer harvests 3600 kg of maize from 2 hectares. Find the yield in kg per hectare, and the yield if the farmer’s neighbour gets 10 000 kg from 4 hectares.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Post-harvest losses
blocks.statement: A village loses a large part of its tomato crop on the way to Yaoundé. Suggest causes and solutions.
steps: Causes: poor roads, no cooling or storage, long delays, careless handling.
Solutions: improved roads, storage and drying, local processing into paste, collective transport.
blocks.answer: Better transport, storage and processing cut losses and improve access.

exercises.prompt: Discuss the causes and consequences of rural-urban migration in a developing country, using Cameroonian examples.
exercises.model: Causes: poor incomes, land shortage and few services in villages push people out; jobs, schools and hospitals in Douala and Yaoundé pull them in. Consequences in towns: pressure on housing and services, informal settlements, unemployment, but also a labour supply and a larger market. In villages: labour shortage and an ageing population, though remittances help families. Balanced rural development is needed.
